title: Brazil’s Open Finance rule separates company consent from approval and assigns responsibility for partner data
summary: The Banco Central do Brasil’s 10 November release explains who is responsible when a company permits its financial data to pass from a participating institution to a commercial partner. Joint Resolution 21 also enables a business to separate a request for data sharing from the approval by an authorised signatory. The resolution’s preamble gives the central bank board’s meeting as 14 October and the National Monetary Council’s as 22 October. It entered into force on publication in the official gazette on 26 October. Those dates matter for interpreting the announcement: publication of the November explanation did not itself start a new consent process at every bank.

The resolution defines the integrating institution as the participant that receives information with the customer’s consent and transmits it to a partner. Before an agreement, the integrator is to assess whether the partner can comply, protect data and maintain controls, with capability attested by an independent auditor registered with Brazil’s securities regulator, the CVM. Express permission must be obtained separately for each partner, in the integrating institution’s own environment. The agreement must allow sharing to stop promptly after a security incident or where compliance is constrained. Further delegation of the partnership and onward sharing with third parties are prohibited. These requirements locate consent and supervisory responsibility at an identifiable institution.

The scope extends beyond handing over a copy of a transaction history. Article 36 covers information derived from analysis or modelling that still identifies, or can identify, an individual or business, including a credit score. It covers sharing with an entity in the same corporate group that lacks central-bank authorisation, while distinguishing an entity acting exclusively as a data processor. The rule also limits processing to the time needed for the authorised purpose and requires deletion at its end in accordance with data protection law. A prospective lender or technology partner must therefore ask what it is receiving, whose customer is identifiable and what its role is before it can assess the value of a data-sharing contract.

For a corporate client, the proposed operational improvement is separation in time and place. A request can begin with the institution seeking the data. Approval can take place later at the transmitting institution, potentially by a different user, without an automatic redirect. That accommodates a business whose employee orders a service and whose treasury signatory approves it. The article states that the regulations create the conditions for Open Finance governance bodies to define technical standards for this workflow. It does not establish how many banks already supported the feature or provide a go-live date across institutions.

The economic mechanism is an information cost in business finance. A firm that can share its banking history more easily may be able to seek quotes from more providers. Tighter partner controls may increase confidence and compliance costs at the same time. The result could differ for larger firms with several signatories and small firms with a single owner-manager. Evidence on completed consents, lender participation, successful credit applications and offered spreads would be needed to decide whether easier data portability translates into stronger competition for borrowers.

There is an earlier, observable implementation step. Article 52-A requires institutions with applicable partnerships already in force at publication to provide the central bank with a list of their partners by 1 December 2026. Information on adapting those contracts and existing consents follows a timetable to be set by the central bank. A submission under that first deadline is evidence that an existing relationship has been reported. It gives no count of companies that have used the new approval sequence or obtained a better credit offer.

questions.question: Which companies actually complete more data-sharing authorisations under the decoupled workflow?
questions.detail: Use verified rollout dates at each institution, and measure initiation, approval, expiry and withdrawal separately. Compare businesses with multiple authorised signatories against similar single-signatory firms, controlling for bank, customer size and seasonality. A rise in starts with unchanged completions would imply that the new workflow addressed a different constraint from the one preventing data from reaching providers.

questions.question: Do new data-sharing relationships expand the effective choice of lender?
questions.detail: Follow completed consents into product quotations and any resulting origination, controlling for borrower risk, maturity, collateral and the reference interest rate. Observe whether new competitors quote or the existing lender simply obtains richer data. The information-sharing reform can change screening or bargaining costs, but the release contains no observed borrowing-rate response and no evidence that all firms benefit equally.

questions.question: Does separate consent for each partner improve customer control at a measurable cost to onboarding?
questions.detail: Compare consent granularity, audit findings, incident response and time to activate new partnerships. Distinguish a shorter approval path for an existing arrangement from the time required to establish one with a new partner. Partner-level permissions and independent capability assessments could affect the number and type of institutions willing to participate, a margin distinct from customer take-up. The 1 December partner inventory is a starting point for this comparison.
